  • Window duration length of 1, 2 ?
  • Infeasible starting point
  • Bad scaling
  • Inversed sign for mean
  • affine expression of x is wrong
  • Input values check
  • SRD needs lower tolerances ? make sure solver tolerance is 1e-6 or a bit lower if dual feasibility is stalling.
  • window for two-sided implementation is too narrow
  • affine expression of x is wrong
  • non-Gaussian distributions?

Common mistakes / issues

Covariance matrix not positive definite

Σ must be symmetric and positive definite. Typical causes are rounding asymmetries, a covariance estimated from too few samples, or duplicated / perfectly correlated components.

isposdef(Σ)                          # check
Σ = (Σ + Σ') / 2 + 1e-10 * I         # symmetrise and add a small jitter

SRD with probabilities below 0.5

SRD requires the mean to be strictly feasible, which in general only holds for p > 0.5. For smaller p, which is rarely of practical relevance, use QMC instead.

Window length of 1 (and 2?)

The window length is κ + 1. With κ = 0 the constraint involves a single component, i.e. it is an individual chance constraint. A closed-form quantile is cheaper and exact, so prefer it (see solve_icc in the portfolio example):

@constraint(model, cash[t] >= quantile(Normal(μ[t], sqrt(Σ[t, t])), p))

<!– TODO: describe what to watch out for with window length 2 –>

Infeasible starting point

Ipopt may fail to converge when started at a point where the chance constraint is badly violated. Start at, or near, a point where the constraint is satisfied, for example the solution of the deterministic problem (all random variables replaced by their mean). In the hydropower example, fill(9.0, T) converges for the single-sided case but not for the two-sided one, which needs [9.0, 10.0, 12.0].

Mean not strictly feasible (SRD)

SRD needs the mean of the random vector to be strictly feasible. Enforce this with a small margin on the affine expressions, for instance for P(ξ ≤ x) ≥ p:

@variable(model, x[i = 1:n] >= μ[i] + 1e-8)

QMC does not need this.

Bad scaling

Ipopt is sensitive to very large or very small numbers in the objective and the constraints. If the solver stalls or reports poor convergence, rescale, e.g. divide the objective by a constant (the portfolio example divides the cost by 1000 and recomputes the true cost afterwards).

Inverted sign of the mean

The constraint is always of the form P(ξ ≤ l(x)) ≥ p (single-sided). If your requirement points the other way, P(ξ ≥ l(x)) ≥ p, rewrite it for -ξ ~ N(-μ, Σ): pass -μ, not μ, together with the same Σ (see the single-sided hydropower example).

slack = [l_0 - l_min - cumx[t] for t in 1:T]    # level_t ≥ l_min  ⇔  -ξ_t ≤ slack_t
add_JCC_QMC(model, slack, [1], T - 1, Σ, -μ, p)

Input values check

Before calling add_JCC_QMC / add_JCC_SRD, check that:

  • 0 < p < 1;
  • Σ is square, positive definite and has the same dimension as μ;
  • every window s:s+κ for s in idx lies inside 1:length(μ);
  • κ is the dimension of the window minus 1, not the number of constraints. With two_sided = true the vector of affine expressions has length 2 × length(μ), stacked as [lower; upper], but κ is unchanged.

Practical tips and workarounds

  • Try QMC first. It has no strict-feasibility requirement and works for single- and two-sided constraints; use SRD for single-sided constraints with p > 0.5.
  • Check the result independently. Estimate the probability at the solution with mvnormcdf or a large Monte Carlo sample on scenarios that were not used in the optimisation, and compare it with p.
  • Make results reproducible. Pass rng = MersenneTwister(seed) to add_JCC_QMC and seed = ... to add_JCC_SRD.
  • Accuracy vs. speed. The number of samples s controls the accuracy of the probability approximation. Increase it if the empirical reliability differs noticeably from p.
  • Non-unique optima. If the objective only depends on a sum of variables, the split between them can be arbitrary and depends on the start value (single-sided hydropower example). Compare objective values, or add a time-varying price to make the solution unique.
  • Compare against the deterministic and individual-constraint models. They show what the joint constraint buys you: the deterministic model violates the requirement often, and individual constraints do not control the joint probability.
  • Silence Ipopt with set_silent(model); ma27 (HSL) is optional: set_optimizer_attribute(model, "linear_solver", "ma27").
